tip: 'Intenté' stays indicative: the trying really happened. 'Por más que' + real past fact = indicative; save the subjunctive for trying that is still hypothetical.
'Sacar adelante' unpacks neatly: 'sacar' (pull out) + 'adelante' (forward) – you haul the family forward through the hardship. Spanish speakers use it for kids, businesses, and projects alike.
Passive with 'ser': 'fue escrito por Cervantes' = it was written by Cervantes – 'ser' + participle + 'por' (agent). Less common than passive 'se'.
'Seguir' + gerund = to keep/continue doing. 'Sigue lloviendo' = it keeps raining.
'Acabo de' is present tense but means the past: 'acabar de' + infinitive = just did. 'Acabo de enterarme' = I just found out – literally 'I finish of finding out'.
Reported question with 'qué': '¿Qué hora es?' → 'qué hora era'.
English says 'as soon as we land' in plain present; Spanish flags it as not-yet-real: 'en cuanto aterricemos' takes subjunctive because the landing hasn't happened.
'Se puso a llorar' = burst into tears: 'ponerse a' + infinitive marks suddenly starting to do something.
No word for 'again' here: 'volver' (to return) + 'a' + infinitive = do it again. 'Volvió a llamarme' = literally 'he returned to calling me' = he called again.
'Serán' is future tense used for probability – conjecture about the present.
'Dejar' means 'leave', so 'no dejo de pensar' is literally 'I don't leave off thinking' – the set way to say 'I can't stop thinking'. No word for 'can' needed.
'De haber sabido' squeezes a whole if-clause into an infinitive: 'de' + 'haber' + participle = 'had I known'. Elegant shortcut for 'si hubiera sabido'.
English needs 'I have been living'; Spanish just carries the time: 'llevar' + time + gerund. 'Llevo tres años viviendo' = literally 'I carry three years living'.
'Andar' + gerund = to go around doing something (habitual/ongoing).
'Hubo' + participle (here 'terminado') = an action finished right before the next. Very formal, literary.
Reported speech: 'cierra' → 'cerraba' (present → imperfect) after 'mencionó que'.
'Si bien' is a formal way to say 'although'.
A past event in present tense? 'Acabo de llegar' is literally 'I finish of arriving' – 'acabar de' + infinitive is how Spanish says 'just did' without any past tense.
'Llevo trabajando' is literally 'I carry working' – Spanish carries a duration into the present, so five years of work needs no 'have been', just 'llevar' + gerund.
'No dejes de practicar': 'dejar' means 'to leave', so Spanish stops actions by leaving them – and the negative works as friendly insistence: be sure to keep practicing.
'Cuando' + subjunctive for future events.
Reported question with 'si': '¿Quieren postre?' → 'si queríamos postre'.
Why 'planifiques', not 'planificas'? 'Por mucho que' concedes any imaginable amount of planning – and unreal, open-ended amounts take the subjunctive.
Reported speech: 'he oído' → 'había oído' (present perfect → pluperfect).
Reported speech: 'estará' → 'estaría' (future → conditional) after 'aseguró que'.
'Gato encerrado' – a locked-up cat? Old Spanish purses were cat-skin 'gatos' kept hidden in clothing, so a shut-in cat means hidden money: a catch you can't see.
'Esa/esta' becomes 'aquella' in reported speech (the more distant 'that').
'Se puso a llorar' – she literally 'put herself to' crying. 'Ponerse a' + infinitive marks bursting into an action suddenly, more abrupt than plain 'empezar'.
Spanish doesn't just regret – it 'repents itself': 'arrepentirse' is always reflexive and needs 'de'. 'Me arrepiento de no haber ido' = 'I repent-myself of not having gone'.
Why 'está', not 'es'? 'Estar' flags a change you can see: 'el jardín está más bonito' = it's looking nicer than last year. 'Es bonito' would just state its permanent character.
